why_it_matters.text: Steeper ramps take more effort to climb. Manual wheelchair users pushing up a {{slope=0.05241|3°}} slope produced significantly higher force, torque and cadence than on the level (36 users with spinal cord injury).

That effort lands on the arms and shoulders. A 2022 systematic review of 34 studies on wheelchair propulsion over slopes, cross-slopes, kerbs and ground types found the topic under-studied and asked researchers to report ramp length and grade consistently so studies can be compared.

People with multiple sclerosis use more energy to walk than people without it, and that extra cost is weakly linked to fatigue (meta-analysis of 9 studies). In one uphill-walking study, 18 people with MS rated uphill effort higher than controls even though their measured oxygen cost was not higher, so how hard a slope feels may not track what it costs.

Going down matters as well as going up. In a transit-ramp trial with 27 users, {{slope=1/12|1:12}} and {{slope=1/8|1:8}} slopes were acceptable to most, but power-chair users and people with vision impairment raised safety concerns about descending steeper slopes.

Being able to climb a short ramp is not the same as managing it all day. A trial of 171 people on {{slope=1/8|1:8}} to {{slope=1/20|1:20}} slopes over 30 ft ({{len=9144|30 ft}}) found only a few manual wheelchair users could not complete an ascent, even at {{slope=1/8|1:8}}. It measured feasibility on one ramp, not repeated or sustained use.

Legal limits are a floor, not a finding. Most codes cap running slope at {{slope=1/12|1:12}}; many lower it for longer runs. Agreement between codes shows what regulators accepted, not what the evidence supports.

universal.statement: No steeper than {{slope=1/20|1:20}} where space allows.
universal.basis: The value in the Guidebook's item register (E-03). The clinical derivation is not yet supported inside the library: the study named as its basis (gap GAP-019) is a backrest-height trial at a single {{slope=0.05241|3°}} slope. Treat as a working position, not a finding.

universal.statement: {{slope=1/12|1:12}} is the most common legal maximum (US, UK, Japan, New Zealand, Canada, Brazil and others).
universal.basis: See the jurisdiction comparison. A legal maximum is a regulatory floor, not a best-practice value.

group.basis: In the library: a 36-person study of wheelchair users with spinal cord injury on level vs a {{slope=0.05241|3°}} slope (higher force uphill), a ramp slope/height/pushing-force study (abstract not retrieved) and a 34-study review. None derives a threshold. Outside the library: a 171-person trial found most could climb {{slope=1/8|1:8}} for 30 ft.

group.who: People with spinal cord injury, especially higher lesions
group.statement: Not set. No SCI-specific threshold has been established.
group.basis: Gap GAP-019 is open. The one SCI slope study in the library enrolled users with lesions at T8-L2 (paraplegia); it does not cover the higher lesions (cervical) whose reduced arm function is the concern.

group.who: People with fatigue-limited conditions (e.g. multiple sclerosis, orthostatic and fatigue conditions)
group.statement: No steeper than {{slope=1/20|1:20}}, with places to rest.
group.basis: This is the mechanism named in the item's title. The library holds no study of MS or fatigue on slopes. Outside the library, MS studies show higher energy cost of walking and higher perceived uphill effort; they do not identify a slope threshold.
The item lists chronic pain as an applicable group but the library holds no pain-specific evidence on ramp gradient (gap GAP-013 is recorded as closed).
A clinical-guideline update on upper-extremity preservation in spinal cord injury is in the library but is not linked to this item.

group.who: Ambulant people using a cane, crutches or walker
group.basis: The item's ramp specification assumes wheelchair use (gap GAP-014, recorded as closed). Studies of gait with a cane or walker on an incline exist outside the library.

person.statement: No general value. The usable slope and length depend on the person's strength, stamina, equipment and the length of the route, so they are set by individual assessment (for example with an occupational therapist) and trial on the actual route.
person.basis: Design at this scale is individual by definition. Evidence on how much people differ: in the 171-person trial the range of tolerated slopes was wide.

evidence.relevance: Only SCI slope study in the library: 36 users, level vs {{slope=0.05241|3°}}, uphill raised force and cadence. Cannot set a threshold from one slope. The register names it as the '1:20 basis' - it is not a threshold derivation.

Systematic review (34 studies) of wheelchair biomechanics on slope, cross-slope, kerb and ground type. The source the gap register itself names for re-research. Not yet linked to this item's BPC; its duplicate record is REF-VERIFIED-003.
Ramp slope, ramp height and pushing force vs wheelchair-driving performance and muscle activity. Participant group not yet confirmed (abstract not retrieved). Duplicate record: REF-00030.
Normative walking energy cost for 260 healthy people. Background for energy arguments; not a disability or ramp study.
Threshold-crossing skill, 214 able-bodied learners in a manual wheelchair: a proxy population, and about thresholds rather than ramp slope.
Clinical-guideline update on upper-extremity preservation in spinal cord injury (consensus). Relevant to why effort on slopes matters; not linked to this item.

excluded_evidence_note: Of the 15 sources linked to this item's BPC, 11 do not concern ramps (6 on stairs; 5 on sit-to-stand, grab bars, luminance contrast, instrumented ADLs). REF-00387 is excluded because its stored title and DOI describe two different papers.

external_evidence.cite: Sanford, Story & Jones (1997). An analysis of the effects of ramp slope on people with mobility impairments. Assistive Technology.
external_evidence.finding: 171 people, slopes 1:8 to 1:20, 30 ft ramp: only a few manual wheelchair users could not ascend, even at 1:8; no change to ADA slope or length recommended.
external_evidence.role: Counter-evidence to treating 1:20 as a feasibility limit for wheelchair users.

external_evidence.cite: Lenker et al. (2016). Usability evaluation of access ramps in transit buses. Journal of Public Transportation.
external_evidence.finding: 27 adults; 1:8 and 1:12 usable and acceptable to most; 1:4 too steep; safety concerns about steep descent among power-chair users and people with vision impairment.

external_evidence.cite: Rooney et al. (2021). Oxygen cost of walking in people with multiple sclerosis and its association with fatigue. International Journal of MS Care.
external_evidence.finding: Meta-analysis, 9 studies: higher oxygen cost of walking in MS; weak association with fatigue.
external_evidence.role: Supports the energy mechanism named in the item.

external_evidence.cite: Har-Nir et al. (2022/23). Energy expenditure and perceived effort during uphill and downhill walking in people with multiple sclerosis. Eur J Phys Rehabil Med.
external_evidence.finding: 18 people with MS: perceived uphill effort higher than controls although oxygen cost was not higher.
external_evidence.role: Partly contradicts a pure energy-conservation rationale.

external_evidence.cite: Liu et al. (2023). Comparison of gait between walking up and down an incline with a walking device in older adults. Geriatric Nursing.
external_evidence.finding: 26 older adults; cane vs rolling walker differ on incline.

jurisdictions.headline: {{slope=1/12|1:12}}
jurisdictions.note: {{slope=1/10|1:10}} or {{slope=1/8|1:8}} only for short rises in limited-space alterations
provisions: {{slope=1/10|1:10}} if the rise is {{len=152.4|6 in}} or less; {{slope=1/8|1:8}} if the rise is {{len=76.2|3 in}} or less.
Top and bottom landings level, at least {{len=1524|60 in}} long and as wide as the ramp; a change of direction needs a {{len=1524|60 in}} by {{len=1524|60 in}} clear landing.
Both sides when the rise is more than {{len=152.4|6 in}}.
Maximum {{slope=1/12|1:12}}, run between landings no more than {{len=9144|30 ft}}, landings at least {{len=1524|60 in}} long.
jurisdictions.vs_guidebook: Allows a slope 67% steeper than the Guidebook position ({{slope=1/20|1:20}}).

jurisdictions.headline: {{slope=1/20|1:20}} (up to 10 m); {{slope=1/12|1:12}} absolute maximum
jurisdictions.note: Steepness depends on length: {{slope=1/15|1:15}} up to 5 m, {{slope=1/12|1:12}} up to 2 m
provisions: {{slope=1/20|1:20}} for a going up to {{len=10000|10 m}} (rise up to {{len=500|500 mm}}); {{slope=1/15|1:15}} up to {{len=5000|5 m}} (rise up to {{len=333|333 mm}}); {{slope=1/12|1:12}} up to {{len=2000|2 m}} (rise up to {{len=166|166 mm}}).

{{slope=1/20|1:20}} is described as preferred; {{slope=1/12|1:12}} as the absolute maximum. One planning document notes slopes steeper than {{slope=1/10|1:10}} are hard for some wheelchair users and can over-balance a chair.
Level, longitudinal slope no more than {{slope=1/60|1:60}}; at least {{len=1200|1200 mm}} long at head and foot; rest places between flights.
jurisdictions.vs_guidebook: The preferred gradient matches the Guidebook position ({{slope=1/20|1:20}}) but only for runs up to {{len=10000|10 m}}.

Handrails where the slope exceeds {{slope=1/12|1/12}} or the height exceeds {{len=160|16 cm}}; tactile warning at the top landing, except for slopes of {{slope=1/20|1/20}} or less.
